explanations.explanation: It turns out that this feature is “noticing” a particular kind of odd‐ball token sequence—a marker that almost always ends up producing the replacement symbol (�) instead of the expected word (like “for”). In other words, the feature is sensitive to the presence of what looks like corrupted or special (often non‐standard or mis‐encoded) textual material that in turn shifts the next–token distribution from a normal word (e.g. “for”) to emitting the replacement character.

It’s a feature that “fires” on end‐of-sentence punctuation—especially the period—that signals a sentence boundary or transition, shifting the context so that without it the model defaults to a generic transitional token like “then.”

It appears that this feature is “noticing” a punctuation‐boundary cue—often a period following an abbreviated or specially formatted token—that signals a switch in the sentence’s (or phrase’s) structural context. In short, it detects when a marker (like the dot after “Gov” or “ST”) that usually indicates an abbreviated term or compound expression is present, which in turn robustly shifts the next‐token prediction; when that signal is removed, the model reverts to a much more generic continuation (e.g. “ableness”).

The feature appears to be sensitive to subword segments that mark off branded or proper‐noun terms—parts of names like “LEGO,” “Mustang,” “NoSQL,” etc.—which in turn condition the model to generate continuations characteristic of product or trademark contexts.

It appears that this feature detects when a token‐segment that would otherwise complete with the common “‑age” ending is instead being used as part of a compound or derived form—essentially signaling a non‐canonical morpheme continuation. In context, when this feature is active the model selects a specialized affix (like “‑ation”, “‑idered”, “‑ind”, etc.) that fits the word’s intended morphology rather than the default “age.”
It appears to be a signal that a token is not an independent word but a subword unit—an affix or fragment that joins with surrounding material to form a compound or morphologically complex word.

This feature detects the punctuation‐based, sentence- or clause-boundary break that signals a shift in discourse—essentially marking the end of one thought and the start of a new segment, which in turn alters the subsequent word choice.

It’s a feature that “lights up” on hyphenated compounds—in other words, it detects the presence of a dash joining word‐chunks (especially in names, adjectives, or compound terms) and uses that signal to adjust how the next token (or subword) is predicted.

This feature activates when a hyphen is used to join word parts—signaling compound construction and morphological concatenation—so that the model treats the attached token as part of a single, compound term (e.g. “zip‑lock,” “fold‑up,” “eye‑catching”), affecting the next token’s prediction accordingly.

It appears that this feature “lights up” on subword fragments—the incomplete morpheme or stem parts of words (often in names, technical terms, or compound expressions) that signal an expected completion. In short, the feature detects when a token is an unfinished word‐piece whose continuation is highly predictable, thereby biasing the next-token prediction toward completing that word.
